meta.title: The Flattery File
meta.subtitle: Spotting, Deflecting, and Deploying the Compliment-Before-the-Ask
meta.description: Every favor-seeker knows the sequence: praise first, ask second. This dossier breaks down how the move works, how to spot it at every stage — same-day, week-later, public — and how to use it yourself without getting caught. Twelve cards. One closed file.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Recognize the Compliment Before the Ask
cards.hook: Someone tells you you're amazing. Then they need something. The compliment was the down payment.
cards.truth:
The flattery-then-ask sequence is the oldest favor-getting move in use today. Most people feel the glow and miss the ask coming.
• The compliment plants a small debt in your head before you know it.
• You feel pushed to say yes because someone 'believed in you.'
• The trap: the bigger the compliment, the harder you'll work to deserve it.
cards.remember: A compliment before a favor is not free. It costs you.
cards.theySee: A colleague smiling and leaning in to tell you how well you handled last week's presentation.

signals.t: They compliment something specific you did when you weren't expecting it.
This person rarely speaks to you but suddenly has a lot to say about your work.
The praise lands right before a decision or a project milestone.
They keep eye contact after the compliment, waiting to see if it landed.

steps.title: Write the compliment down word for word
steps.desc: On your phone or a notepad. The exact words. This separates the warm feeling from the data.

steps.title: Note who said it and when
steps.desc: Time-stamp it. If an ask follows within a week, you have your pattern.

steps.title: Wait 30 seconds before you respond
steps.desc: Smile, say thanks, and say nothing else. Give them space to show the next card.

cards.counter:
Someone is softening you up with praise before making an ask. Notice the lift in your mood — that's the hook.
• The praise felt sudden or very specific to a recent win.
• Say 'thanks' and go quiet. Let them fill the silence.
• Ask yourself what they might want before they say it.
cards.insight: The debt from flattery is invisible until the ask lands — then it's obvious. The harder question is whether you spotted it before you agreed.

cards.title: Watch for the Ask That Comes a Week Later
cards.hook: They complimented you at the party. A week later, they emailed. The gap was not an accident.
cards.truth:
Delaying the ask after the flattery is a deliberate move. The longer the gap, the harder the connection is to see.
• Praise plants a seed; time lets you forget it was planted.
• When the ask arrives, you remember a good feeling, not where it came from.
• The tell: the ask feels out of nowhere but somehow comfortable.
cards.remember: Late asks after early praise are still the same move.
cards.theySee: A coworker who complimented their leadership skills at a company dinner last Friday, now in their inbox asking for a reference.

signals.t: Praise was given at a social event; an ask arrives 5 to 10 days later.
Their follow-up email is suddenly warm but gets to a request fast.
They mention the earlier praise as if reminding you of a bond you share.
The request is larger than your relationship warrants but arrives like a small thing.

steps.title: Start a short log of compliments from frequent contacts
steps.desc: Name, what they said, the date. Patterns appear within a week.

steps.title: When the ask arrives, re-read the compliment
steps.desc: Look at what they praised. Does it map directly to what they're now asking you to do?

steps.title: Write yes or no on paper before you open a reply window
steps.desc: Don't let the inbox push you. Decide first, then respond.

cards.script: "Before I answer — what made you think of me for this?"
cards.counter:
Someone primed you with praise days ago and now they're collecting.
• The ask feels weirdly comfortable even though it's large.
• Say 'let me get back to you' and wait 24 hours before deciding.
• Re-read what they said. Ask if you'd say yes without the warmth attached.
cards.insight: The time gap is the move. Widen it enough and the flattery becomes a background feeling you can't trace. The next card is how to name it out loud and watch what breaks.

cards.title: Flattery Hits Harder When You Have Power
cards.hook: The more power you have, the more you believe the praise is real. Power doesn't protect you from flattery — it makes you a better target.
cards.truth:
Leaders and high-status people are flattered more often and believe it more. Their position creates the blindspot.
• Status makes you think you earned the praise, so you stop checking.
• Flatterers read your ego faster than your peers do.
• Observers watching you fall for it will think you're naive — not strong.
cards.remember: The higher you are, the more people below you want something.
cards.theySee: A manager nodding along while a junior employee praises their decision-making in front of the team.

signals.t: Someone compliments your judgment in a group setting right before asking for a favor.
A much-lower-ranked person approaches you one-on-one with an unsolicited compliment.
They wait until you're alone to say something flattering.
They specifically compliment your influence, reach, or ability to make things happen.

steps.title: Audit your last three yes decisions that followed praise
steps.desc: Write down the last three times someone complimented you and then you granted something. Look at the pattern.

steps.title: Ask a peer what they observed in the room
steps.desc: Pick someone who was there. Ask: 'Did that look like a setup?' Listen without defending yourself.

steps.title: Set a 48-hour rule for any request that follows a compliment
steps.desc: For the next 30 days, any ask that arrives after praise gets a two-day wait before you answer.

cards.script: "I appreciate that. I'll need a day before I can give you an answer."
cards.counter:
Someone is using your status against you — they know you want the praise to be true.
• The compliment was specifically about your power, judgment, or access.
• Name it quietly: 'I notice you said that right before asking me something.'
• Strip the warm feeling. Decide as if the praise never happened.
cards.insight: Research shows observers rate leaders as weaker when they grant favors right after being flattered. What you gain in the room you may lose in the building — and you won't see it go.

cards.title: Know Who Praises Everyone Before You Trust Anyone's Praise
cards.hook: Some people hand out compliments to every person in the room. Their praise means less. The person who almost never says anything nice — when they do, pay attention.
cards.truth:
Praise only carries weight relative to the person giving it. Context is everything.
• A serial flatterer's words are cheapened by their own pattern.
• Rare praise from a quiet person is almost always genuine.
• The trap: serial flatterers still make each target feel singled out.
cards.remember: Learn who praises everyone before you trust anyone's praise.
cards.theySee: A coworker who hands out compliments to every person in the room, now telling you specifically that your report was excellent.

signals.t: This person compliments multiple people in the same conversation or meeting.
The compliment could apply to anyone — 'you're so capable,' 'you're amazing.'
The colleague who rarely says anything positive suddenly singles you out.
They praised someone else five minutes ago; now the praise is all for you.

steps.title: Build a mental file on three frequent contacts today
steps.desc: For each: do they praise freely or rarely? Note it. This is your baseline for reading their future words.

steps.title: When praised, check it against the baseline
steps.desc: Does this person say this to everyone? If yes, note the praise but don't change your behavior.

steps.title: Watch who they praised before coming to you
steps.desc: If they complimented someone else in the last hour, the warmth now running your way is manufactured.

cards.script: "You say that to a lot of people — what do you actually need?"
cards.counter:
Someone is using serial praise to blur the signal so you can't tell what's real.
• Their words are warm but vague enough to apply to anyone in the room.
• Smile, say thanks, and give them nothing extra.
• File the pattern. Use it to read them faster next time.
cards.insight: The real problem isn't the serial flatterer — it's your own need to feel singled out. That's the hole they fill every time, and they found it faster than you did.

cards.title: Say 'You Flatter Me' and Watch Their Face
cards.hook: Three words end the game early. 'You flatter me.' Name what they're doing and they have to recalibrate.
cards.truth:
Naming the flattery forces the other person to either own it or back off. Both moves give you information.
• The label makes the invisible visible without accusing anyone directly.
• An honest person laughs it off. A strategic one flinches or doubles down.
• After the label, the ask — if it was coming — arrives with less force.
cards.remember: Name what they are doing before they get to the ask.
cards.theySee: A person who was building toward a request, now pausing after you said 'you flatter me.'

signals.t: They blink more than usual right after you name the flattery.
They laugh immediately — louder than the moment warrants.
They shift the subject quickly, as if you broke a script they were running.
They insist the compliment is genuine and get slightly defensive about it.

steps.title: Use the phrase the moment the compliment lands out of place
steps.desc: When the praise feels sudden or unearned, say it right there: 'You flatter me.' Flat tone. No smile needed.

steps.title: Watch the three seconds after you say it
steps.desc: Their face tells you more than their next sentence. Flinch means strategic. Laugh means comfortable. Silence means they're recalculating.

steps.title: Let them lead the next sentence
steps.desc: Don't fill the quiet. Wait. If an ask was coming, it arrives awkward. Awkward asks are easier to decline.

cards.counter:
Someone named your flattery before you reached the request. You're on record as having a motive.
• Don't over-explain. More words now make you look more guilty.
• Own it or laugh it off — either is better than a long defense.
• Pivot directly: 'Fair enough — here's what I'm actually looking for.'
cards.insight: The label doesn't stop the ask. It just makes the ask cost more. The real move is what you do with the awkward second that follows — and most people waste it.

cards.title: Never Agree to a Big Ask While the Praise Is Still Fresh
cards.hook: Your best decisions don't happen in the same room where you got the praise. Get out of the room first.
cards.truth:
The warm feeling from a compliment fades. Decisions made while that feeling peaks favor the flatterer, not you.
• The feeling is strongest in the first ten minutes after praise. Yes lives there.
• By the next morning, the ask looks different without the warmth attached.
• The trap: they push for an answer before the feeling fades. That pressure is the tell.
cards.remember: Never agree to a big ask while the praise is still warm.
cards.theySee: A person waiting for your answer, watching you nod along while the good feeling from their praise is still in the air.

signals.t: They say they need an answer today or this week, right after praising you.
They make the ask face-to-face, not over email, to keep the warmth in play.
They call a large request 'just a small thing' right after the compliment.
After the compliment they go quiet and wait, giving you space to fill with a yes.

steps.title: Say 'I'll get back to you' every single time without exception
steps.desc: Not 'probably yes.' Not 'I think so.' The phrase is: 'I'll get back to you.' End there.

steps.title: Sleep on it literally
steps.desc: Give the ask at least one night. Write the question on paper before bed. Read it cold in the morning.

steps.title: Write your answer alone with no one in the room
steps.desc: Draft the reply by yourself. No warmth left over. Ask: what do I actually want to give here?

cards.script: "I need to check a few things — I'll get back to you tomorrow."
cards.counter:
Someone is using the warmth from flattery to close you fast. Time pressure right after praise is the clearest tell.
• They praised you and immediately needed an answer.
• Say 'tomorrow' every time without giving a reason for the delay.
• Notice if they push back hard. That push means the timing was planned.
cards.insight: Loss aversion works both ways here. They're afraid you'll cool off. You're afraid of seeming ungrateful. Both fears serve the flatterer — and only one of you knows that going in.

cards.title: The People Watching Think You Got Played
cards.hook: You said yes after the praise. You felt generous. The people in the room filed you as easy to work.
cards.truth:
Observers rate leaders as weaker when they grant favors right after being flattered. The target never sees this cost.
• You feel warm and giving. The room notices you're easy to soften.
• Word spreads: this person can be warmed up before an ask.
• The real cost isn't the favor granted — it's the signal sent to everyone watching.
cards.remember: What felt generous in the moment looked weak to the room.
cards.theySee: Other team members watching a manager agree to a request seconds after a junior praised them in front of the group.

signals.t: Others in the room make brief eye contact with each other while you agree.
The conversation shifts right after you say yes, as if something was settled and filed.
Other people start praising you more in the days and weeks that follow.
Someone references the exchange in a later conversation with a slight smile.

steps.title: Replay the last public favor you granted after being praised
steps.desc: Did it follow a compliment? Who was in the room? Would they call you easy to work with? Be honest.

steps.title: Change the visible pattern once this week
steps.desc: Next time you're praised in public, delay or decline the follow-up ask. One shift resets the signal.

steps.title: Name your reason out loud when you do grant a favor
steps.desc: Say why you're saying yes — not because of the compliment, but the merits. Separate them visibly in front of the room.

cards.script: "The compliment's appreciated, but let me look at this on its own merits."
cards.counter:
You're being used to signal to a room that you're approachable and easy to soften.
• Notice who's watching when the flattery happens.
• What you agree to in public sets what others think they can ask for.
• One public refusal resets expectations faster than three private ones.
cards.insight: The most dangerous cost is the one you don't see. You leave the room satisfied; others leave with a read on you. The harder move is managing what you look like — not just what you decided.

cards.title: Give the Compliment First, Then Wait Before You Ask
cards.hook: If you need something, don't open with the ask. Open with something true about them, then wait. Days if you can.
cards.truth:
Flattery-then-ask works because the praise plants a small debt before the ask arrives. Most people use the sequence too fast.
• Same-day praise followed by an ask is readable. Anyone paying attention sees it.
• Give the compliment at a neutral moment — not right before you need something.
• When the ask comes later, they feel a warm pull they can't quite trace back to you.
cards.remember: Give the compliment now. Ask for something later. Never together.
cards.theySee: A colleague they spoke to last week who said something kind about their work, now in their inbox with a request.

signals.t: A genuine opening to compliment their work presents itself with no ask in sight.
Days after you praised them, they reference what you said in passing.
They receive the praise without any tension, because no ask follows immediately.
Sometimes they offer to help before you ask — the debt is already sitting with them.

steps.title: Find one true thing to praise and say it today
steps.desc: Not vague. Something specific: 'The way you handled that client in the call was sharp.' Write it out before you say it.

steps.title: Deliver it with nothing attached then stop
steps.desc: Say it. Walk away. No 'by the way.' No transition to your need. Let it sit alone.

steps.title: Mark the ask date on your calendar for 3 to 5 days from now
steps.desc: Put it on your calendar. Different channel if possible — email after an in-person compliment. The gap hides the sequence.

cards.script: "That brief you put together last week was the clearest thing in that room. Wanted to say it."
cards.counter:
Someone praised you at a neutral moment with nothing following. That doesn't mean it's free.
• Notice if the praise was specific and unsolicited with no obvious reason.
• Don't feel the debt just because they were generous. Wait and see what arrives.
• When the ask comes, treat it on its merits. Strip the warmth out before you answer.
cards.insight: The gap between praise and ask is the variable most people skip. Close it and the move is obvious. Widen it and you're invisible — which is where the real upper hand sits.

cards.title: Specific Work Praise From the Wrong Person Is Still a Setup
cards.hook: Not all flattery hits the same nerve. Praising your work is harder to dismiss than praising your personality. The person asking knows which one you'll believe.
cards.truth:
Work praise — 'your analysis was excellent' — feels earned, so your guard drops before you check if it's real.
• Work praise maps to something real and specific. That's exactly why it works better.
• Excessive work praise — more than the work warrants — is still a setup.
• The tell: the praise is more specific than your relationship with them justifies.
cards.remember: Specific work praise from the wrong person is still a move.
cards.theySee: A junior colleague going through their recent report with unusually detailed praise, right before they need something.

signals.t: They reference a detail of your work that most people wouldn't have noticed or remembered.
The compliment is stronger than the work — the work was decent; they call it exceptional.
This person never commented on your work before; now they have a lot to say.
They email the compliment, which feels more formal and carries more binding weight.

steps.title: Ask yourself if this person reads your work normally
steps.desc: If the answer is no, the specific praise is suspicious. Mark it in your log with the date.

steps.title: Check whether the praise maps to the ask
steps.desc: Write down what they praised. Write down what they asked for. If they line up directly — it was deliberate.

steps.title: Reply to the praise and leave the ask unanswered
steps.desc: Respond: 'Thanks for that.' Stop there. See if the ask resurfaces separately. Answer it without the warmth attached.

cards.script: "I appreciate that — what specifically made you think of me for this?"
cards.counter:
Someone praised something real in your work to make the setup feel deserved.
• The more specific the praise, the harder it is to dismiss. That's exactly why they used it.
• Separate the compliment from the request in your head before you answer either one.
• A strong compliment about your work does not make the request more valid.
cards.insight: The hardest flattery to spot is the kind that's partly true. The gap between accurate praise and accurate praise used as a tool is small — and the person using it knows exactly where that line sits.

cards.title: Grant the Favor on Your Terms, Not Theirs
cards.hook: Sometimes the ask is reasonable and you'll say yes. How you say yes matters more than that you said yes.
cards.truth:
Saying yes while naming your terms cuts the debt they built with the flattery. It separates what you give from why they thought you'd give it.
• Giving without naming your terms signals the move worked on you.
• 'Yes — and here's what I need back' resets the balance in the room.
• The favor is the same. The reading of you is not.
cards.remember: Say yes on your terms, or they'll take the credit for why you agreed.
cards.theySee: The person who asked, now hearing your yes alongside a condition they didn't expect.

signals.t: When you add a condition, they pause — the yes was supposed to be simple.
They agree to your condition quickly without thinking — they just want the yes.
They come back later to work around your condition, once they already have the favor.
The follow-up thank-you is warmer than the favor warrants — they know the move worked.

steps.title: Name one thing you want in return before you open the reply
steps.desc: Not punishment — something reasonable. Write it down before you type a single word in response.

steps.title: State your condition as part of the yes
steps.desc: Say: 'Yes — and I'll need X from you when the time comes.' Clean, simple, no apology.

steps.title: Track whether they deliver on your condition
steps.desc: Put a calendar reminder. If they don't follow through, you have data on how much the flattery was worth to them.

cards.script: "Yes — and I'll need you to return the favor when I come back to you. Fair?"
cards.counter:
Someone attached a condition to your ask after you used flattery to soften them. They caught the move.
• The yes came with a string. That means they knew what was happening in the room.
• Don't rush to agree to the condition. Think about whether the trade is worth it.
• If the condition feels too heavy, say no to the whole thing. The flattery doesn't obligate you.
cards.insight: The condition you attach is a signal — to them and to anyone watching — that the compliment didn't close the deal alone. That's the part that matters for the next time they decide whether to approach you.

cards.title: Public Praise in a Group Is Almost Always a Setup
cards.hook: They praised you in front of everyone. Now the ask is coming. And everyone is watching to see if you'll say no.
cards.truth:
Public flattery adds an audience to the debt. Saying no in front of people feels like rejecting their public judgment of you.
• In private you can decline cleanly. In public, a no embarrasses you both.
• They chose the open setting deliberately. The audience is the pressure.
• You're committed in two directions now: to them and to the room's read of you.
cards.principle: Cialdini: Social Proof — Public Commitment Trap
cards.remember: They brought an audience to the compliment for a reason.
cards.theySee: A group of coworkers watching a colleague praise someone at a team meeting, then pivot directly to a request.

signals.t: The compliment arrives at the start or middle of a group meeting, not in a private hallway.
People around you visibly agree with the praise, making you feel publicly backed.
The request is delivered facing the group, not just you — the room becomes part of the pressure.
Others react positively to the praise before any request, making a refusal feel disruptive to everyone.

steps.title: Name the setting before you answer anything
steps.desc: Say: 'I'd want to talk through the details outside of this room.' Move the ask to private ground.

steps.title: Thank them for the praise and visibly separate it from the ask
steps.desc: 'Thanks — let's connect after this meeting on the specifics.' Say it in front of the room.

steps.title: Make the actual decision alone after the room empties
steps.desc: The audience pressure dissolves when people leave. Decide then — not while anyone is watching.

cards.script: "I appreciate that — let's talk after the meeting about what you're looking for."
cards.counter:
Someone chose a room full of people to make your refusal cost more. The praise was the price of admission.
• They didn't ask in private because private has no audience to hold you accountable.
• Move the conversation one-on-one. The ask shrinks by half when the room empties.
• What you agree to in public is harder to walk back. Delay first, every time.
cards.insight: The audience isn't there by accident. The next question is whether you move the conversation to your own ground — or let them run it in the open while everyone watches.

cards.title: Praise Them for Free and Watch Who Starts Calculating
cards.hook: Want to know if someone runs the flattery game on you? Praise them first — with nothing attached — and watch how they react when no ask follows.
cards.truth:
A genuine person receives a compliment and lets it sit. A strategic flatterer receives one and immediately starts working out what they owe you.
• The strategic one will praise you back right away or get slightly nervous.
• They're waiting for your ask. When it doesn't come, they don't know what to do with the debt.
• Praise with no ask attached is a read — and sometimes the most disarming move you have.
cards.remember: Praise for free and watch who starts calculating.
cards.theySee: A person they've been managing carefully, who just gave them a specific compliment with nothing following it.

signals.t: They return a compliment right away — balancing the ledger in real time.
They ask 'is there something you need?' because praise without an ask feels wrong to them.
They don't know how to respond to praise that expects nothing back.
They contact you a day or two later, still trying to work out what you wanted.

steps.title: Pick one person you suspect is running the flattery game on you
steps.desc: Think about who has praised you recently with no ask arriving yet. Choose one person.

steps.title: Give them a genuine specific compliment today with no ask attached
steps.desc: One real thing they did well. Say it directly. Stop there. No request, no transition, no 'by the way.'

steps.title: Observe for the next 24 to 48 hours
steps.desc: Do they immediately return a compliment? Do they ask if you need something? That's your read on how they operate.

cards.script: "That approach you took on the pricing problem was sharp. Just wanted to say it."
cards.counter:
You just received a compliment with no ask attached and you feel slightly off-balance about it.
• Genuine praise doesn't need a reaction. Strategic praise waits for one.
• If you feel like you owe them something, ask yourself why — no ask was made.
• Let it sit. If they follow up with a request, you have your answer.
cards.insight: Praise with no ask is either the most generous thing someone can give you or the most patient setup. The difference only shows up later — and by then you've already filed the person correctly.
